title: Heavy Duty Arm Day (Hypertrophy Log #1)
summary: First Hypertrophy Log: NH films and explains a home-gym arm day built as two giant sets (EZ curl, lying power lateral raise, cable rear-delt spread, band pushdown, weighted sit-up; then triceps dips, heavy dumbbell pullover, rope rear-delt row, hammer preacher curl). He explains warm-ups, partial ranges that keep tension, negatives, training around elbow tendinitis and a neck nerve issue, and his 6-8 exercise, 2-4 sets, 3x/week upper structure.
claims: The weight lifted is irrelevant; what matters is choosing a load that takes you to failure and progressing
His warm-up: mess around, warm up tendons, then do the first heavy lift itself for about two sets (empty bar, then 50 lb) before working sets
He prefers a narrow grip on curls for his build and stops short of full extension at the bottom with shoulders high to keep the biceps engaged and avoid rebounding
Negatives should stay the same speed or slow down as a set goes on; speeding up means you rely on momentum
His training is 100% giant sets with no rest between exercises; on arm day you should not be winded after curls
Lying lateral power raises with momentum give a great side-delt stretch but are for advanced lifters only; beginners can hurt themselves
Supersetting the same muscle twice (stretch then contraction movement) is only for fairly advanced lifters
Order exercises in a giant set by descending intensity so the most demanding lift gets peak energy
Use a wrist-roller handle on band pushdowns so grip does not fail before the triceps
He has right-elbow tendinitis from close-grip bench, so he swapped skull crushers and French presses for band pushdowns
Train around pain rather than skipping a muscle so the pain eventually goes away
A band's ascending resistance puts most tension near lockout, making band pushdowns easy on the elbows while hitting the long head
He does weighted sit-ups with feet under the rack, slow tempo, 6-12 reps to failure
Each giant set: 3-4 rounds with about 2 minutes rest between rounds; the first giant set takes around an hour
Triceps dips: keep the torso vertical, initiate by breaking the elbows and stop when the humerus is parallel to the floor to limit chest and shoulder involvement
Do triceps isolation before dips when you have elbow problems to get fluid into the tendons
Arm days should also include compounds, and everything should be taken to failure; do not treat arm day as an easy day
An arm day can and should include some upper-back work; the pullover hits the triceps long head, lats and upper back
On pullovers, do not go into full shoulder extension; that disengages the lats and is why people feel it in the shoulder joint
Dips followed by pullovers is a double chest stretch that left him with upper-chest soreness; may be counterproductive for less advanced lifters
Rear-delt rope rows: keep the inner forearm flush with the biceps at the top rather than flaring the elbow far back
Being able to refocus between exercises is the hard part of giant sets; many people sandbag because they can only give 100% to one exercise
Have fun in the gym; if you don't enjoy training you won't stick to it
Hammer-grip preacher curls with a towel are S tier for forearms and brachioradialis; stop slightly below parallel to avoid overextending the tendon
Single-arm work lets you put 100% of the intensity on one arm, key for massive biceps and forearms
His forearms improved a lot in six months purely from isolation
Upper body days have 6-8 exercises, 2-4 sets each, three times a week
exercises: narrow grip; stop short at bottom; shoulders high; slow last negative
lie on bench; let weight drop under bench for stretch; forearm in line with arm
vertical torso; elbows break first; stop at humerus parallel
get in position by sitting with dumbbell then leaning back; no full shoulder extension
lats, triceps long head, upper back
inner forearm flush with biceps at top; slow negative
towel grip; stop below parallel; slow negative
